title: IBD Distilling Qualifications Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: What the Institute of Brewing and Distilling distilling qualifications cover, who each level suits and how to prepare from India.
teaser: The IBD ladder runs from a first certificate to Master Distiller. Here is which rung a career changer should aim for first.
standfirst: The Institute of Brewing and Distilling sets the best known exams in the trade. They are respected because they are hard. For someone moving into whisky from another career, knowing which level to sit first saves a year of wasted effort.
sections: The IBD is an examining body, not a school

The Institute of Brewing and Distilling (IBD) is a London based professional body with roots going back to the nineteenth century. It writes syllabuses and sets exams. It does not, on the whole, teach you. Candidates study on their own or through a course provider, then sit the exam at an approved centre on a fixed date.

That split matters for a career changer in India. You can register from Bengaluru or Delhi, but you need a plan for the learning itself. The IBD publishes a syllabus and recommended reading for each qualification. Treat that syllabus as the contract: if a topic is on it, it can be examined.

Always check the current syllabus, exam dates and centre list on the IBD website before you start. The structure has been revised over the years and will be again.

The distilling ladder has three broad rungs.

  • General Certificate in Distilling. The entry level. It covers raw materials, mashing, fermentation, distillation, maturation and packaging at an overview depth. It suits operators, new joiners, sales and marketing staff who need to talk credibly about production.
  • Diploma in Distilling. The professional qualification, taken in modules with written exams. It goes deep into process science and plant: enzyme behaviour in the mash, yeast metabolism, still design, reflux and cut points, cask chemistry. It suits shift leads, QC staff and assistant distillers.
  • Master Distiller. The top level, aimed at people who already run production. It tests judgement across the whole operation, including management, quality systems and troubleshooting.

Most career changers should start at the General Certificate. It gives the vocabulary that every later level assumes.

The entry exam rewards breadth. You need to know, for example, that a malt whisky wash typically sits around 8% ABV, that a pot still run splits into foreshots, heart and feints. You need to know that ethanol boils at 78.4 °C against water's 100 °C. You need to explain why worts for malt whisky are not boiled, so enzymes survive into the washback.

The Diploma rewards mechanism. Knowing that copper removes sulphur compounds is entry level. Explaining why a tall still with a rising lyne arm gives a lighter spirit, in terms of reflux and the boiling points of different congeners, is Diploma level. Calculation questions appear too: spirit yield in litres of pure alcohol per tonne, dilution to a filling strength, losses in the cask.

For a chemistry or engineering graduate, the science is rarely the problem. The plant knowledge is. People who have never stood next to a wash still struggle to answer questions about foaming, charge volumes or condenser performance with any confidence.

A few practical points for candidates here:

  • Book early. Exam centres and dates are limited, so check where the nearest approved centre is before you commit to a sitting.
  • Get floor time. A week shadowing at a malt distillery, a grain plant or even a brewery teaches the equipment far faster than a textbook.
  • Learn in metric and in ABV. The exams use litres, degrees Celsius and percentages. Proof belongs to history and the American trade.
  • Expect Scotch as the default example. Indian molasses spirit, six row barley and hot climate maturation will mostly be your own homework, so read our guide to the angels' share in Indian heat alongside the set texts.

Budget several months of steady study for the General Certificate if you work full time. The Diploma modules each need a good deal longer.
How it fits next to a degree or a short course

The IBD qualifications are not the only route. Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh runs well known degrees in brewing and distilling. A short applied course teaches the hands-on side faster than any exam does. Our guide to studying distilling and the qualifications that count compares the options.

The pattern we see work best is simple: a short practical course first so the words have pictures attached, then the General Certificate to formalise it, then the Diploma once you hold a production role. Going straight to the Diploma with no plant experience is the most common way to fail it.
Study habits that get people through

Candidates who pass tend to share a few habits. They study a little most days rather than cramming in the last month. They practise past style questions under timed conditions, because writing a clear answer in a few minutes is a skill of its own. They draw the process as a flow diagram from memory, from milling through to cask filling, until every vessel and every strength is in the right place.

They also work the numbers by hand. If a cask holds 200 litres at 63.5% ABV, it holds 127 litres of pure alcohol. If 5,000 litres of wash sits at 8% ABV, it carries 400 litres of pure alcohol into the wash still. Calculations like these appear in some form at every level. They are easy marks for anyone who has practised them.

Download the current General Certificate in Distilling syllabus from the IBD website. Go through it line by line and mark each topic green, amber or red for how well you could explain it to a colleague. Anything red on fermentation or distillation is where a structured course pays for itself, because those are the sections that carry the most marks and the most jargon.
faqs: Which IBD distilling qualification should I take first?
Most people new to the trade should start with the General Certificate in Distilling. It covers the whole process at overview depth and every later level assumes it.
Can I sit IBD exams in India?
The IBD runs exams at approved centres in several countries. Check the IBD website for the current centre list and dates before you register.
Do I need a science degree for the Diploma in Distilling?
It helps with the chemistry and calculations, but plant experience matters as much. Candidates without floor time usually find the equipment questions hardest.
